title: Java (8 → 25)
description: Write modern Java confidently and know what every release from 8 to 25 added — so you can read any codebase, legacy or brand new, and pick a version.
keyIdeas: Compare objects with `.equals()`, not `==` — and remember that Strings never change, methods return new ones.
Program to interfaces: `List`, `Set` and `Map` (with `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, `HashMap`) cover most everyday needs.
Java 8's lambdas, streams and `Optional` are the baseline of every modern codebase.
A new Java ships every March and September; most teams move along the LTS jumps 8 → 11 → 17 → 21 → 25.
Modern Java models data with records, sealed types and pattern-matching `switch`.
Virtual threads (Java 21) let simple blocking code scale to huge numbers of concurrent tasks.

concepts.label: Primitives vs references
concepts.summary: A primitive variable holds the value itself and any other variable holds a reference, and both assignment and argument passing copy whichever one it holds (Java is pass-by-value).

concepts.label: Immutable strings
concepts.summary: A String never changes, so methods like replace() return a new string you must keep, and a StringBuilder is the mutable choice for building text in a loop.

concepts.label: == vs equals()
concepts.summary: On objects == asks whether two references point to the very same object, while equals() compares content, so compare strings with equals().

concepts.label: Access modifiers
concepts.summary: private, package-private, protected and public control who can see a member, and keeping fields private makes other classes go through methods.

concepts.label: Inheritance & interfaces
concepts.summary: A class extends one class and implements many interfaces, can @Override inherited methods, and the object's real type decides which method runs.

concepts.label: Collections & generics
concepts.summary: List for order, Set for uniqueness and Map for lookup by key, declared by interface and typed with generics like List<String>, which only take reference types.

concepts.label: Checked vs unchecked
concepts.summary: Checked exceptions (Exception but not RuntimeException, like IOException) must be caught or declared with throws, while unchecked ones need neither.

concepts.label: try-with-resources
concepts.summary: A finally block always runs before the method returns, and resources declared in a try header are closed automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown.

concepts.label: LTS releases
concepts.summary: A new Java ships every March and September, but only the long-term-support releases (8, 11, 17, 21, 25) get years of fixes and run in production.

concepts.label: Preview features
concepts.summary: Big features ship first as previews that are off by default and need --enable-preview, and a feature only counts from the release where it became final.

concepts.label: Lambdas
concepts.summary: A lambda like x -> x * 2, or a method reference like String::length, implements a functional interface: an interface with exactly one abstract method.

concepts.label: Streams
concepts.summary: A stream is a lazy, single-use pipeline: a source, intermediate operations like filter and map, then one terminal operation that runs it.

concepts.label: Optional
concepts.summary: Optional<T> is a return type for "maybe no value", handled with map, orElse and ifPresent instead of returning null or calling get() blindly.

concepts.label: var
concepts.summary: var lets the compiler infer a local variable type from its initializer, but the type is still fixed at compile time and var needs an initializer.

concepts.label: Switch expressions
concepts.summary: A switch with case ... -> arrows returns a value, never falls through, and uses yield for block results, unlike the old colon-and-break switch.

concepts.label: Records
concepts.summary: A record is a concise immutable data class whose constructor, accessors like p.x(), equals, hashCode and toString are generated from its components.

concepts.label: Immutable List.of
concepts.summary: List.of, Set.of and Map.of (Java 9) build unmodifiable collections, so add or put compiles but throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime.

concepts.label: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: Patterns test a value's type and bind its parts in one step: instanceof String s (16), then switch type patterns with when guards and record patterns (21).

concepts.label: Compact source files
concepts.summary: Since Java 25 a whole program can be a file with just void main() { IO.println(...); }, with no class or public static boilerplate.

concepts.label: Version timeline
concepts.summary: Each release has a headline feature (8 lambdas, 10 var, 16 records, 21 virtual threads, 25 compact files), and code needs the version where its features became final.

concepts.label: ExecutorService
concepts.summary: An ExecutorService runs submitted tasks on its threads and hands back a Future whose get() blocks for the result, and shutdown() stops new tasks while letting queued ones finish.

concepts.label: Race conditions
concepts.summary: When threads share mutable state, read-modify-write steps like count++ interleave and lose updates, so use atomics, locks or no sharing at all.

concepts.label: CompletableFuture
concepts.summary: A CompletableFuture describes what happens next without blocking: thenApply transforms, thenCompose chains another async call, thenCombine merges two, exceptionally recovers.

concepts.label: Virtual threads
concepts.summary: Virtual threads (Java 21) are cheap JVM-managed threads, so you run one per blocking task without pooling them; they speed up waiting, not CPU-bound work.

units.title: Java essentials
units.description: The core of the language you'll use in every Java file: types, strings, classes, collections and exceptions.

lessons.title: Program structure, primitives & references
lessons.takeaway: Primitives hold values; everything else holds a reference — and assignment copies whichever one the variable holds.

steps.title: The smallest classic program
Primitives vs references
steps.body:
Java has **8 primitive types**: `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`. A primitive variable holds the **value itself**.

Everything else — `String`, arrays, collections, your own classes — is a **reference type**. The variable holds a *reference* (an arrow) to an object living on the heap.

Assignment always copies what the variable holds. For a primitive that's the value; for a reference it's the arrow, so two variables can end up pointing at the **same object**.

Each primitive has a wrapper class (`int` → `Integer`), and Java converts between them automatically (*autoboxing*).

steps.title: Copying a value vs copying a reference
steps: `int b = a` copies the **value** 5 into `b`. Changing `b` later doesn't touch `a`, so `a` is still 5.
`int[] y = x` copies the **reference**. There is still only one array, and both `x` and `y` point at it.
`y[0] = 99` changes that shared array, so `x[0]` is now 99 too.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Which division happens first — and with which types?
steps.explanation: `total / count` is `int / int`, which is **integer division**: 7 / 2 = 3. Only then is 3 widened to the `double` 3.0. Fix it with `(double) total / count`, which gives 3.5.

steps.prompt: Java passes arguments **by value**. What does this print?
steps.hint: What gets copied into the parameter in each case: a value, or a reference?
steps.explanation: The first `reset` gets a copy of the number 5 and changes only its own copy. The second gets a copy of the **reference**, which still points to the caller's array, so `arr[0] = 0` changes the real array. Result: `5 0`.

steps.prompt: Step into `change`. Java copies each argument: for an array, it copies the **reference**. Predict the values when asked.

frames.note: Inside `change`: `arr` and `nums` point to the same array.
`arr` now points to a brand-new array.

steps.explanation: `arr` starts as a copy of the reference in `nums`, so `arr[0] = 99` changes the one array both point to. `n` is a copy of `count`, so `n = 99` can't touch `count`. `arr = new int[]{7, 7}` points the **copy** at a new array; `nums` still points at the old one. Output: `99 1`.
steps.hint: Ask yourself which object each variable points to. Changing an object is visible through every reference; reassigning a variable isn't.

steps.prompt: `StringBuilder` is a *mutable* text buffer. What does this print?
steps.explanation: `a` and `b` are two references to the **same** `StringBuilder`. Appending through `b` changes the object that `a` also sees, so it prints `hi!`.

steps.prompt: This should sort a copy and leave `original` untouched, printing `3 1`. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 2 to `int[] sorted = Arrays.copyOf(original, original.length);`
Change line 2 to `int[] sorted = new int[3]; sorted = original;`
steps.hint: After line 2, how many arrays exist?
steps.explanation: `int[] sorted = original` copies the **reference**, not the array: there is still only one array, and `Arrays.sort(sorted)` sorts it in place, so `original[0]` is 1 as well. `Arrays.copyOf(original, original.length)` builds a second array with the same values, and only that copy gets sorted. `final` only stops `original` from pointing at a different array — its contents can still change. A cast copies nothing, and `sorted = original` throws away the fresh `new int[3]` and points at the shared array again.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.code: System.out.println(10 / 4);
steps.explanation: Both operands are `int`, so this is integer division: the fractional part is dropped and 10 / 4 = **2**. Write `10 / 4.0` to get 2.5.

lessons.title: Strings, immutability & == vs equals
lessons.takeaway: Strings never change — keep the result of every String method — and compare content with `.equals()`, never `==`.

steps.title: Strings are immutable
steps.body:
A `String` object can **never change**. Methods like `toUpperCase()`, `replace()`, `trim()` or `concat()` don't modify the string — they **return a new one**.

That makes strings safe to share between objects and threads, but it creates a classic bug: calling a String method and forgetting to use the result.

When you build a long string piece by piece in a loop, use a `StringBuilder` instead of `+=` — each `+=` copies the whole string again.

steps.title: The forgotten result
steps: Line 2 creates a new string `"JAVA"` — and throws it away. `s` still refers to `"java"`.
So the first `println` prints `java`.
Line 4 stores the new string back into `s`. Now `s` refers to `"JAVA"`.

steps.title: == vs .equals()
steps.body:
- For **primitives**, `==` compares values: `3 == 3` is true.
- For **objects**, `==` asks *"are these the very same object?"* — it compares references.
- `.equals()` compares **content**, as defined by the class. `String`, `Integer`, `List` and records all define it sensibly.

Rule: **compare objects with `.equals()`**. Sometimes `==` on strings appears to work because identical literals are shared, but that's luck, not a guarantee.

If a value might be `null`, write `"admin".equals(name)` or `Objects.equals(a, b)` — calling `.equals` on `null` throws a `NullPointerException`.

steps.prompt: What does this print? Type each printed line on its own line.
steps.explanation: `new String(...)` always creates a distinct object, so `a == b` (same object?) is **false**. The characters are identical, so `a.equals(b)` is **true**.

steps.prompt: This should print `Welcome, admin`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.hint: `toLowerCase()` returns a new string. Is it the same object as the literal `"admin"`?
steps.explanation: `toLowerCase()` builds a **new** `String` object containing `admin`. `==` asks whether `input` and the literal are the very same object, and they aren't, so it goes to `else`. `.equals()` compares the characters and gives `true`. Swapping the sides of `==` still compares references, `final` doesn't change what `==` means, and `trim()` has no whitespace to remove — the strings were never the problem, the comparison was.

steps.prompt: `name` comes from user input and might be `null`. Which check is correct **and** can never throw?
steps.explanation: `"admin".equals(name)` calls the method on a literal that is never null, and simply returns false when `name` is null. `name.equals(...)` and `name.compareTo(...)` throw a NullPointerException for null, and `==` compares references, not content.

steps.prompt: You build a 10,000-line report inside a loop. What's the best way to accumulate the text?
choices: Append to a `StringBuilder`, then call `toString()` once
Use `==` to check for duplicates first
steps.explanation: Because strings are immutable, each `+=` copies everything built so far — O(n²) work overall. A `StringBuilder` appends in place. (And `concat` without assigning does nothing useful: the result is thrown away.)

steps.prompt: Strings never change; methods return new ones. Step through and predict each value when asked (quotes optional).

frames.note: The uppercase copy was created and thrown away.
`u` and `s` point to the same string object.

steps.explanation: `s.toUpperCase()` on line 2 builds `"JAVA"` and throws it away: `s` is untouched. Line 3 keeps the result in `t`. `s = s + "!"` makes a new string and points `s` at it. `u = s` copies that reference, so when line 6 points `s` at yet another new string, `u` still refers to `"java!"`.
steps.hint: A String method never changes the string it's called on. Only `=` changes what a variable points to.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Was the result of `replace` stored anywhere?
steps.explanation: `replace` returned `"bat"` but nobody kept it, so `s` is still `"cat"`. Then `s + "s"` is assigned back, giving **cats**.

steps.prompt: What does this print? Type each printed line on its own line.
steps.hint: `a + "!"` builds a new string. Which variables point at it?
steps.explanation: `b = a` makes both variables point at the same `"Hi"` object. `a + "!"` can't change that object (strings are immutable), so it creates a new `"Hi!"` and only `a` is moved to it. `b` still points at `"Hi"`. The lengths are 3 and 2, and `+` between two `int`s adds them: `5`.

lessons.title: Classes, interfaces & inheritance
lessons.takeaway: Keep fields private, extend one class, implement many interfaces — and the object's real type decides which method runs.

steps.title: A class bundles data and behaviour
Access modifiers
steps.body:
From most to least restrictive:

- `private` — only inside the same class
- *(no keyword)* — package-private: classes in the same package
- `protected` — same package plus subclasses
- `public` — everyone

The usual habit: **fields private**, expose behaviour through methods. That's why `Account` has `getBalance()` and `deposit()` instead of a public `balance` field — the class can enforce rules like "no negative deposits".

`static` members belong to the class itself rather than to each object.

steps.title: Inheritance and interfaces
steps.body:
- A class can **extend one** class: `class Dog extends Animal`. It inherits fields and methods and can **override** them (mark with `@Override`).
- A class can **implement many** interfaces: `class Circle implements Shape, Comparable<Circle>`. An interface is a contract — a list of methods a class promises to provide.
- `super.method()` calls the parent's version.

**Polymorphism:** a variable's *declared* type decides which methods you may call; the object's *actual* type decides which implementation runs. Program to interfaces: `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`

steps.title: Which method runs?
steps: The declared type is `Animal`, so the compiler allows the call: `Animal` has a `sound()` method.
At runtime the object is a `Dog`. The JVM looks up the method on the **actual** object (*dynamic dispatch*).
`Dog` overrides `sound()`, so its version runs.

steps.prompt: The last three lines are in a **different class** from `Counter`. They should count one click and print `1`, but the code doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error: count has private access in Counter
fixes: Change line 2 to `private static int count;`
steps.explanation: `count` is `private`, so only code inside `Counter` can touch it — even just reading it from another class fails to compile. Go through the public method instead: `c.get()`. That's exactly the point of encapsulation. `c.count()` doesn't exist (Java doesn't generate getters for you), and making the field `static` or reaching it through the class name doesn't change the fact that it's `private`.

steps.prompt: Which declaration is legal Java?
choices: `class A extends B implements C, D {}`
steps.hint: How many classes can you extend? Which keyword comes first?
steps.explanation: A class extends **at most one** class and may implement any number of interfaces, with `extends` written before `implements`. Interfaces extend other interfaces (`interface I extends J`); they never `implements`.

steps.prompt: What does this print? Type each printed line on its own line.
steps.explanation: The object is a `Child`, so `Child.hello()` runs. Its first line calls the parent's version (`Base`), then it prints `Child`.

steps.prompt: `Shape` is an interface. Fill in the keyword: `class Circle ______ Shape { ... }`
steps.explanation: Classes **implement** interfaces and **extend** classes.

lessons.title: Collections & generics
lessons.takeaway: List for order, Set for uniqueness, Map for lookup by key — declared by interface, typed with generics.

steps.title: The big three
steps.body:
- **`List`** — ordered, allows duplicates, access by index. Default: `ArrayList`.
- **`Set`** — no duplicates. `HashSet` (no order), `LinkedHashSet` (insertion order), `TreeSet` (sorted).
- **`Map`** — key → value lookup. `HashMap` (no order), `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap` (sorted by key).

Declare variables by the interface and pick the implementation once:

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, Integer> ages = new HashMap<>();
```

Iterate with for-each: `for (String n : names)`, and for maps `for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : ages.entrySet())`.

steps.title: Generics
steps.body:
The `<String>` in `List<String>` is a **type parameter**. The compiler then guarantees that only strings go in, and you get strings out — no casts, no surprises at runtime.

- The **diamond** `<>` on the right lets the compiler infer the type: `new ArrayList<>()`.
- Generics work only with **reference types**: write `List<Integer>`, not `List<int>`. Autoboxing converts between `int` and `Integer` for you.
- Without generics ("raw types", pre-2004 code) everything is `Object` and needs casts — avoid them.

steps.title: Counting words with a Map
steps: The first time a word is seen, `getOrDefault` returns 0, so the count is stored as 1.
Each later time, the existing count is read and `put` overwrites it with count + 1.
`"a"` appears three times.
steps.answer: It prints `3`. (Printing the whole `HashMap` would show the keys in no guaranteed order.)

steps.explanation: A `Set` ignores duplicates — the second `add("x")` returns false and changes nothing. Size: **2**.

steps.prompt: This should print `7`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
error: unexpected type
  required: reference
  found:    int
fixes: Change line 1 to `List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();`
Change line 1 to `ArrayList<int> nums = new ArrayList<>();`
Change line 1 to `List<Int> nums = new ArrayList<>();`
steps.explanation: Type arguments must be reference types. Use the wrapper `Integer` instead of `int`; autoboxing handles the conversion when you add and read numbers.

steps.prompt: You need to find a `User` by their email address, fast, many times per second. Which collection fits?
steps.explanation: A `HashMap` gives O(1) average lookup by key and returns the `User` itself. Searching a list is O(n), and a set of emails only tells you whether the email exists.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: A `TreeMap` keeps its keys **sorted** (alphabetically for strings), so `Al` comes before `Zoe` regardless of insertion order. A `HashMap` would give no guaranteed order.

steps.prompt: This should remove the empty names, but it crashes. Click the line that causes the crash.
steps.hint: A for-each loop walks the list with an iterator. What happens to that iterator when the list changes underneath it?
steps.explanation: A for-each loop uses an iterator, and `ArrayList`'s iterator fails fast: if the list is changed by anything other than the iterator itself, the next step throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. `removeIf` removes matching elements safely in one call. Removing by index still modifies the list mid-loop, and `List.of` is immutable, so `remove` would throw `UnsupportedOperationException` instead. (An explicit `Iterator` with `it.remove()` also works.)

lessons.title: Exceptions & try-with-resources
lessons.takeaway: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; use try-with-resources so anything you open gets closed.

steps.title: Checked vs unchecked
steps.body:
- **Checked exceptions** — subclasses of `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`, like `IOException`. They model things that can go wrong outside your control. The compiler **forces** you to either `catch` them or declare `throws IOException` on the method.
- **Unchecked exceptions** — subclasses of `RuntimeException`, like `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException`. Usually bugs or bad input; no declaration required.
- **Errors** like `OutOfMemoryError` — don't catch these.

`finally` blocks always run, whether the `try` succeeded, threw, or returned.

steps.title: Tracing try / catch / finally
steps: `trying` is printed.
`Integer.parseInt("x")` throws a `NumberFormatException` (unchecked), so the `return` in the `try` never completes.
The matching `catch` prints `bad input` and prepares to return -1.
Before the method actually returns, `finally` runs and prints `done`.

steps.title: try-with-resources

steps.prompt: Calling `readConfig("")` should print `failed: no path`, but the code doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
error: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown
error: exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement
2 errors
fixes: Change line 1 to `static String readConfig(String path) throws IOException {`
Change line 3 to `throw new RuntimeException("no path");`
Change line 1 to `static String readConfig(String path) throws RuntimeException {`
steps.hint: Is `IOException` checked or unchecked? What does the compiler demand for checked ones?
steps.explanation: `IOException` is **checked**: a method that throws it must declare `throws IOException` (or catch it itself). Once line 1 declares it, both errors disappear: the caller's `catch (IOException e)` now has something to catch, and the program prints `failed: no path`. Throwing a `RuntimeException` instead makes the method compile, but then catching `IOException` is an error because nothing in the `try` can throw it. Catching `Exception` in main doesn't fix `readConfig` itself, and declaring `throws RuntimeException` says nothing about `IOException`.

steps.prompt: A method throws each of these and has no `try`. Sort them: does the compiler make it declare `throws`?
steps.hint: Unchecked exceptions extend `RuntimeException` and usually mean a bug or bad input. Checked ones come from the world outside your code: files, databases, other threads.
steps.explanation: **Checked**: `IOException`, its subclass `FileNotFoundException`, `SQLException` and `InterruptedException` extend `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`, so `javac` says *unreported exception ...; must be caught or declared to be thrown*. **Unchecked**: `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException` and its subclass `NumberFormatException`, `ArithmeticException` (`1 / 0` on `int`s) and `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` all extend `RuntimeException`. So does `UncheckedIOException`, despite its name: it exists to wrap an `IOException` *without* forcing every caller to declare it.

steps.prompt: What does this print? Type each printed line on its own line.
steps.hint: Resources are closed in the opposite order to how they were opened.
steps.explanation: The body runs first, then resources are closed in **reverse** order of declaration: B, then A. That way a resource that depends on an earlier one is closed first.

steps.prompt: What does `System.out.println(test());` print?
steps.hint: `finally` runs before the method hands its return value back to the caller.
steps.explanation: The `catch` computes the return value `"caught boom"`, then `finally` prints `finally ` **before** `test()` returns. Only then does `println` print the returned string: **finally caught boom**.

units.title: Modern Java, version by version
units.description: How Java releases work, and what each LTS jump from 8 to 25 brought — so you can read any codebase and pick a version.

lessons.title: Release cadence & LTS
lessons.takeaway: A new Java ships every March and September, but the versions that matter are the LTS jumps: 8, 11, 17, 21, 25.

steps.title: A new Java every six months
steps.body:
Java 8 came out in 2014 and Java 9 in September 2017 — big, slow releases. Since **Java 10 (March 2018)** there's a new feature release **every March and every September**, like clockwork:

- 10 → March 2018, 11 → September 2018
- 17 → September 2021, 21 → September 2023
- 25 → September 2025

The old "1.8" naming is gone: it's just Java 21, Java 25. Each release is smaller, so features arrive steadily instead of in one giant drop every few years.

steps.title: LTS: the versions teams actually run
steps.body:
A non-LTS release is only updated until the next one arrives — six months. **Long-Term Support (LTS)** releases get security and bug fixes for years from Oracle and other vendors (Eclipse Adoptium, Amazon Corretto, and others).

**LTS versions: 8, 11, 17, 21, 25.** Since 17, a new LTS arrives every two years (every fourth release).

Most companies jump from LTS to LTS. That's the 80/20 of versions: learn what each **LTS jump** bundled — 8 → 11 → 17 → 21 → 25 — and you can read almost any codebase.

steps.title: Preview features
steps.body:
Big language features usually arrive as a **preview** first: fully implemented, but allowed to change. They're off by default; you must opt in at compile time and run time:

```
javac --release 25 --enable-preview Main.java
java --enable-preview Main
```

A feature typically goes preview → second preview → **final** over a few releases. (New APIs can also start even earlier as *incubator* modules under `jdk.incubator`.) Once final, it's standard Java — no flags. In this course, "added in version N" means **final** in N unless it says preview.

steps.title: Picking a version for a new project
steps.problem: You're starting a new backend service today (late 2026). Which Java version should you target?
steps: Prefer an **LTS** so you get years of updates without upgrading every six months.
The newest LTS is **25** (September 2025); 21 is the one before it.
Check that your frameworks, libraries and build tools support it. If a key dependency doesn't yet, fall back to 21.
steps.answer: Target the **newest LTS your dependencies support** — usually 25, otherwise 21. Stay off non-LTS versions unless you're happy to upgrade every six months.

steps.prompt: Java 22 was released in March 2024. When was Java 23 released?
steps.explanation: Releases come every six months, March and September, so 22 → March 2024 and 23 → **September 2024**. Then 24 in March 2025 and 25 in September 2025.

steps.prompt: Your company only allows LTS versions in production. Sort these releases: which ones may you deploy?
steps.hint: Since 17, an LTS arrives every two years, which is every fourth release.
steps.explanation: The LTS releases are **8, 11, 17, 21 and 25**. Versions like 9, 10, 15, 22 and 24 were each supported only until the next release six months later, so running one of them in production means upgrading every six months to keep getting security fixes.

steps.prompt: Since Java 17, every fourth release (one every two years) has been an LTS: 17, 21, 25. If the pattern holds, which version is the next LTS after 25?
steps.explanation: 25 + 4 = **29**, due two years after 25 (September 2027).

steps.prompt: On JDK 25 you compile code that uses a feature which is still a **preview** in 25. Compilation fails, saying preview features are disabled. What's the fix?
choices: Add a `@Preview` annotation to the class
steps.explanation: Preview features must be explicitly enabled with `--enable-preview` at **both** compile time (together with `--release`/`--source` for that exact version) and run time. Code using previews is tied to that one JDK version.

lessons.title: Java 8: lambdas, streams & Optional
lessons.takeaway: Java 8 made functions first-class: lambdas plug into functional interfaces, and streams describe data pipelines instead of loops.

steps.title: Lambdas and functional interfaces
steps.body:
Java 8 (2014, LTS) is the biggest release in Java's history and the baseline of every modern codebase.

A **functional interface** has exactly one abstract method: `Runnable`, `Comparator<T>`, `Function<T, R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, `Consumer<T>`. A **lambda** is a compact implementation of that one method:

```java
Predicate<String> isLong = s -> s.length() > 5;
Function<String, Integer> len = s -> s.length();
```

A **method reference** is an even shorter lambda that just calls a method: `String::length`, `System.out::println`, `Integer::sum`.

steps.title: Sorting before and after Java 8
steps.problem: Sort a `List<String> names` by length. How does the code change from Java 7 to Java 8?
steps: `Comparator` has one abstract method, so a lambda can replace the class: `names.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()));` — `List.sort` itself is new in Java 8.
`Comparator.comparing` builds the comparator from a key extractor, and a method reference supplies the key.

steps.title: Streams
steps.body:
A **stream** is a pipeline over data: a source, then *intermediate* operations, then one *terminal* operation.

```java
List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 3)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

- Intermediate ops (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) are **lazy** — nothing happens until a terminal op runs.
- Terminal ops (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`, `sum`, `findFirst`, `reduce`) produce the result.
- Streams never modify the source and can be used only once.

steps.hint: Keep the even numbers, square them, add them up.
steps.explanation: The evens are 2, 4, 6. Squared: 4, 16, 36. Sum: **56**.

steps.title: Optional, java.time and default methods
steps.body:
- **`Optional<T>`** — a return type for "maybe no value", instead of returning `null`. `findFirst()` returns one. Use `map`, `orElse`, `orElseGet`, `ifPresent` rather than calling `get()` blindly.
- **`java.time`** — `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `ZonedDateTime`. Immutable and clear; it replaces the old `Date` and `Calendar`.
- **Default and static interface methods** — interfaces can now contain method bodies. That's how `List.sort` and `Collection.stream()` were added without breaking every existing implementation.
- **`CompletableFuture`** — async pipelines (covered in the Concurrency unit).

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: No fruit starts with "b", so `findFirst()` returns an empty `Optional`. `map` on an empty Optional stays empty, and `orElse(0)` supplies the fallback: **0**.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Does this pipeline have a terminal operation?
steps.explanation: `peek` and `filter` are intermediate, lazy operations. With no terminal operation, the pipeline never runs, so only `end` is printed.

steps.prompt: This should print `2 of 3`, but it crashes. Click the line that causes the crash.
steps.error:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed
    ...
fixes: Change line 2 to `final Stream<String> s = words.stream();`
Change line 4 to `long total = s.filter(w -> true).count();`
steps.hint: Line 3 ends with a terminal operation. What state is `s` in afterwards?
steps.explanation: A stream can be used **only once**. Line 3 runs the pipeline to its terminal `count()`, which uses `s` up, so any further operation on it — even another `filter` or `collect` — throws `IllegalStateException`. Ask the source for a fresh stream instead: `words.stream()`. `final` only stops the variable being reassigned; it doesn't make the stream reusable.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (Write the date as Java prints it.)
steps.code: System.out.println(LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31).plusMonths(1));
steps.hint: There's no February 31st — and 2024 is a leap year.
steps.explanation: `java.time` clamps to the last valid day of the month, and 2024 is a leap year, so you get **2024-02-29** (ISO format `yyyy-MM-dd`).

lessons.title: Java 9–11: var, factories & nicer strings
lessons.takeaway: The 8 → 11 jump brings `var`, immutable `List.of`/`Map.of`, handy String and Files methods, and a built-in HttpClient.

steps.title: Java 9 (2017)
steps.body:
- **Module system (JPMS)** — a `module-info.java` declares what a module `requires` and `exports`. It restructured the JDK itself; many applications never write a module.
- **JShell** — an interactive REPL: type `jshell` and try code line by line.
- **Collection factories** — `List.of(1, 2, 3)`, `Set.of("a", "b")`, `Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2)`. They're **immutable** and reject `null`.
- Stream additions: `takeWhile`, `dropWhile`, `ofNullable`, and `Stream.iterate` with a stop condition.
- Private methods in interfaces, and try-with-resources on an existing effectively-final variable.

steps.title: Java 10 (2018) and 11 (2018, LTS)
steps.body:
**Java 10** — the first six-month release — added **`var`** for local variables:

```java
var names = new ArrayList<String>();   // type: ArrayList<String>
```

The type is still fixed at compile time; `var` just saves typing. Locals only (not fields or parameters), and it needs an initializer. Also: `List.copyOf`, `Optional.orElseThrow()`, `Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()`.

**Java 11 (LTS)** added String `isBlank()`, `lines()`, `strip()`, `repeat(n)`; `Files.readString`/`writeString`; the standard **`HttpClient`** (`java.net.http`); `var` in lambda parameters; `Optional.isEmpty()`; and running a source file directly: `java Hello.java`.

steps.title: Rewriting Java 8 code in Java 11
steps: Immutable list → the Java 9 factory: `var tags = List.of("a", "b");`
Read a whole file as a String → Java 11: `var text = Files.readString(Path.of("notes.txt"));` (UTF-8 by default).
"Only whitespace?" → Java 11: `boolean empty = text.isBlank();` (and it understands Unicode whitespace, which `trim()` doesn't).

steps.explanation: `List.of` returns an **immutable** list. The type is still `List`, so `add` compiles, but calling it throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Use `new ArrayList<>(List.of(...))` when you need to modify it.

steps.prompt: On Java 11, this should print `12`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
error: cannot infer type for local variable total
  (cannot use 'var' on variable without initializer)
steps.explanation: `var` infers the type from the initializer, so `var total;` has nothing to infer from — declare the type yourself. `null` has no useful type either, `final` doesn't add one, and `var total = ""` makes `total` a `String`, so assigning an `int` to it fails. `var` works for local variables and loop variables like the for-each one.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.code:
String s = "  hi  ";
System.out.println("[" + s.strip() + "]" + "-".repeat(3));
steps.explanation: `strip()` (Java 11) removes leading and trailing whitespace, and `"-".repeat(3)` gives `---`. Result: `[hi]---`.

steps.prompt:
What's the **minimum** Java version that compiles this line?

```java
long n = Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt")).lines().count();
```
steps.hint: Look up when `Files.readString` and `String.lines()` appeared.
steps.explanation: `Files.readString`, `Path.of` and `String.lines()` were all added in **Java 11**. On Java 8 you'd need `Files.readAllBytes` or `Files.lines`.

lessons.title: Java 12–17: switch, text blocks, records & sealed types
lessons.takeaway: The 11 → 17 jump modernizes data code: switch expressions, text blocks, records, instanceof patterns and sealed types.

steps.title: Switch expressions (final in 14)

steps.prompt: Here's an old-style switch with no `break`s. What does it print?
steps.hint: Without `break`, where does execution go after a case?
steps.explanation: Old colon-style cases **fall through**: execution starts at `case 6` and keeps running every following case. That bug-prone behavior is exactly what arrow-style `case 6 ->` removes.

steps.title: Text blocks (15), records and instanceof patterns (16)
steps.body:
**Text blocks** (final in 15) are multi-line strings; common indentation is stripped:

```java
String json = """
    {
      "name": "Ada"
    }
    """;
```

**Records** (final in 16) are concise immutable data classes:

```java
record Point(int x, int y) {}
```

You get private final fields, a constructor, accessors `x()` and `y()`, plus `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`.

**Pattern matching for instanceof** (16) tests and casts in one step: `if (obj instanceof String s) { ... s.length() ... }`. Java 16 also added `Stream.toList()`.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: Records generate `equals` that compares the components, so two points with the same values are equal. The generated `toString` uses the format `Point[x=3, y=4]`.

steps.prompt: This should move the point to x = 10 and print `Point[x=10, y=4]`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error: cannot assign a value to final variable x
fixes: Change line 4 to `p = new Point(10, p.y());`
Change line 3 to `Point p = new Point(3, 4);`
steps.hint: What kind of fields does a record generate?
steps.explanation: Record components become **private final** fields, so a record can't be changed after it's built. To "change" one, create a new record with the new value and copy the rest: `new Point(10, p.y())`. Records have no setters, `p.x()` is a method call that returns a value (you can't assign to it), and `var` versus `Point` makes no difference — the field is still final.
Pattern matching for `instanceof` adds a binding variable after the type. `s` is in scope (already cast) wherever the test is known to be true.

steps.title: Sealed classes (final in 17)

steps.prompt:
What's the minimum Java version that compiles this **without preview flags**?

```java
record User(String name) {}

String greeting = """
    Hello
    """;
```
steps.hint: Text blocks and records became final in different releases. The later one wins.
steps.explanation: Text blocks are final in 15, but records only became final in **16** (they were previews in 14 and 15). Code needs the version where *all* its features are final.

steps.prompt: Given `record Book(String title, int pages) {}` and `var b = new Book("Dune", 412);`, write the expression that returns the title.
steps.explanation: Record accessors are named exactly after the components — **`b.title()`**, not `getTitle()`.

lessons.title: Java 18–21: pattern matching & virtual threads
lessons.takeaway: Java 21 finalizes the modern toolkit: pattern-matching switch, record patterns, virtual threads and sequenced collections.

steps.title: 18, 19, 20: the run-up
steps.body:
- **18** — **UTF-8 is the default charset** everywhere (no more files that read differently on Windows), the `jwebserver` command serves static files for quick tests, and Javadoc gained `@snippet`.
- **19** — virtual threads and record patterns arrive as **previews**.
- **20** — scoped values as an incubator API, plus further previews of the pattern and virtual-thread features.

The big features of these releases became final in the next LTS — **21**. That's why many teams jumped straight from 17 to 21.

steps.title: Pattern matching for switch + record patterns (21)
Virtual threads & sequenced collections (21)
Rewriting an instanceof chain
steps: Each `instanceof` + cast becomes a **type pattern** in a `case`: `case String s -> ...`.
The `i > 100` condition becomes a **guard**: `case Integer i when i > 100 -> "big number";`.
Order matters: the guarded case must come **before** the plain `case Integer i`, or the compiler reports it as unreachable (dominated).
`Object` isn't sealed, so a `default` is required.

steps.prompt: What does this print on Java 21?
steps.explanation: `42` is autoboxed to an `Integer`. The first case's guard (`i > 100`) is false, so the next case `Integer i` matches: `int 42`.

steps.prompt: On Java 21, this should print `big` (250 is over 100), but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label
fixes: Change line 4 to `case Integer j when j > 100 -> "big";`
steps.hint: Can the second case ever be reached?
steps.explanation: An unguarded `case Integer i` matches **every** Integer, so a later `case Integer i when ...` could never run. The compiler rejects it as *dominated*. Put more specific cases first.

steps.prompt: What does this print on Java 21?
steps.code:
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(list.getLast() + list.reversed().getFirst() + list.getFirst());
steps.explanation: `getLast()` is `c`; the first element of the reversed view is also `c`; `getFirst()` is `a`. Concatenated: **cca**.

steps.hint: This isn't a plain type pattern — it deconstructs the record.
steps.explanation: `obj instanceof Point p` works from 16, but deconstructing with a **record pattern** `Point(int x, int y)` was a preview in 19 and 20 and became final in **21**.

lessons.title: Java 22–25: simpler programs
lessons.takeaway: Java 22–25 cut ceremony: `_` for unused variables, stream gatherers, and Java 25's `void main()` compact source files.

steps.body:
- **22** — **unnamed variables & patterns**: write `_` for things you must declare but never use: `catch (NumberFormatException _)`, `case Circle(_) ->`. Also the **Foreign Function & Memory API** (call native C libraries without JNI) and launching **multi-file** programs with `java Main.java`.
- **23** — **Markdown documentation comments** with `///`. (String templates had been previewed in 21–22 but were withdrawn — they are *not* part of Java.)
- **24** — **stream gatherers** (`Stream.gather`, custom intermediate operations), virtual threads no longer get pinned inside `synchronized`, the Class-File API, and the Security Manager is permanently disabled.

steps.title: Java 25 (LTS): compact source files
steps.body:
A complete Java 25 program can be just this file, `Hello.java`:

```java
void main() {
    IO.println("Hello, Java 25!");
}
```

Run it with `java Hello.java`.

- No class declaration, no `public static`, no `String[] args`.
- `IO.println`, `IO.print` and `IO.readln` cover simple console input and output.
- A compact source file automatically imports everything in the `java.base` module, so `List`, `Map` and friends need no imports.

Instance `main` methods also work in ordinary classes. It's the friendliest the language has ever been for beginners and scripts.

steps.title: More of Java 25
A stream gatherer (24)
steps.problem:
What does this print on Java 24+?

```java
List<List<Integer>> windows = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    .gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2))
    .toList();
System.out.println(windows);
```
steps: `gather` plugs a custom intermediate operation into the stream; `Gatherers` ships ready-made ones.
`windowFixed(2)` groups elements into lists of 2, in order: `[1, 2]`, `[3, 4]`.
The last window may be smaller: `[5]`.
`toList()` (Java 16) collects the windows.
steps.answer: `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]` — something that was awkward with plain Java 8 collectors.

steps.hint: Look at the catch parameter.
steps.explanation: The unnamed variable `_` was a preview in 21 and became final in **22**. Everything else here works on Java 9+. (It prints `1`.)

steps.prompt: Which of these is a **complete file** that runs with `java Hi.java` on Java 25 and prints `Hi`?
steps.explanation: A compact source file still needs a `main` **method** with a return type, but it can be an instance method with no parameters and no enclosing class. Java doesn't allow bare top-level statements.

steps.prompt: This compact source file, `Hello.java`, should print `Hi Ada` and then `Hi Linus` on Java 25, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
error: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   method println(String)
  location: class Hello
steps.hint: A compact source file imports classes like `List` automatically. Does that include methods?
steps.explanation: A compact source file automatically imports the **classes** of `java.base` — that's why `List` works — but not a bare `println` method. Console output goes through the `IO` class: `IO.println(...)`. `import module java.base;` imports the same classes again, not methods; making `main` static changes nothing about name lookup; and `println` lives on `System.out`, not `System`. (Early previews in Java 23–24 did allow a bare `println`; the final Java 25 version dropped it.)
Before flexible constructor bodies, `super(...)` had to be the very first statement. The feature was previewed in 22–24 and became final in **25**.

steps.prompt: This is a complete Java 25 compact source file. What does it print?
steps.explanation: `List` needs no import in a compact source file. `reversed()` (Java 21) gives `[java, modern]`, `getFirst()` is `"java"`, uppercased: **JAVA**.

lessons.title: Every version at a glance: 8 → 25
lessons.takeaway: Know one headline per version, and remember that a feature counts from the release where it became final.

steps.body:
- **8** (2014, LTS) — lambdas, streams, `Optional`, `java.time`, default methods
- **9** (2017) — modules, JShell, `List.of`/`Map.of`
- **10** (2018) — `var`
- **11** (2018, LTS) — `isBlank`/`strip`/`repeat`, `Files.readString`, `HttpClient`, `java Hello.java`
- **12** (2019) — switch expressions (preview), `Collectors.teeing`
- **13** (2019) — text blocks (preview), `yield`
- **14** (2020) — switch expressions final, helpful NullPointerExceptions
- **15** (2020) — text blocks final, sealed classes (preview)
- **16** (2021) — records, `instanceof` patterns, `Stream.toList()`

- **17** (2021, LTS) — sealed classes, strongly encapsulated JDK internals
- **18** (2022) — UTF-8 by default, `jwebserver`, `@snippet`
- **19** (2022) — virtual threads and record patterns (preview)
- **20** (2023) — scoped values (incubator), more previews
- **21** (2023, LTS) — virtual threads, pattern-matching switch, record patterns, sequenced collections
- **22** (2024) — unnamed `_`, Foreign Function & Memory API
- **23** (2024) — Markdown doc comments `///`
- **24** (2025) — stream gatherers, no pinning in `synchronized`
- **25** (2025, LTS) — compact source files, `import module`, flexible constructors, scoped values

steps.prompt: A library's README says "requires Java 16+". Which feature is it most likely using?
steps.explanation: Records became final in **16** — a common reason for a 16+ requirement. Lambdas are 8, `var` is 10 (both work on 16 but don't require it), and virtual threads need 21.

steps.prompt: This codebase must still compile on **Java 9** (`javac --release 9`) and print `14 false`. Click the line that has to change.
steps.error:
warning: as of release 10, 'var' is a restricted type name and cannot be used for type declarations or as the element type of an array
error: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   class var
fixes: Change line 4 to `long n = Stream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2).limit(7).count();`
steps.explanation: `var` arrived in **10**. `List.of` and the three-argument `Stream.iterate` are Java 9; `Optional.ofNullable` is Java 8.

steps.prompt: A program reads files with `new FileReader(file)` (no charset given). Accented letters come out garbled on some older Windows machines but not on Linux. From which version is the default charset UTF-8 on every platform?
steps.explanation: Before **18**, the default charset depended on the operating system's locale — often not UTF-8 on Windows. Java 18 made UTF-8 the default everywhere. (Passing a charset explicitly is still clearest.)

steps.prompt: Your team is stuck on **Java 20**. Which of these can you use without `--enable-preview`?
steps.hint: Three of these were still previews in 19 and 20.
steps.explanation: `jwebserver` shipped in **18**. Virtual threads, record patterns and pattern-matching `switch` were all previews in 19–20 and only became final in 21 — one more reason teams went from 17 straight to 21.

steps.prompt: You see comments starting with `///` above methods in a new codebase. What are they?
steps.explanation: Java **23** lets you write Javadoc in Markdown with `///` lines. String templates were previewed in 21–22 and then withdrawn, so they aren't in Java at all.

steps.prompt: Which Java version introduced lambdas and the Stream API? (Just the number.)
steps.explanation: **Java 8** (2014, LTS). Any codebase older than that uses anonymous classes and loops instead.

units.title: Concurrency
units.description: Running work in parallel: executors, async pipelines and Java 21's virtual threads.

lessons.title: Threads & ExecutorService
lessons.takeaway: Submit tasks to an ExecutorService instead of managing threads, and never share mutable state without atomics or locks.

steps.title: Threads and executors
steps.body:
A **thread** runs code at the same time as other threads: `new Thread(() -> work()).start();`.

In real code you rarely create threads by hand. An **`ExecutorService`** owns a pool of threads; you **submit tasks** and get back a `Future` — a handle to the result that will arrive later.

- `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` — n reusable threads
- `submit(task)` → `Future<T>`; `future.get()` waits for the result
- `shutdown()` — accept no new tasks; let submitted ones finish

Since Java 19, an `ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable`: in try-with-resources, closing waits for all tasks.

steps.title: Getting a result from another thread
steps: `submit` hands the lambda (a `Callable<Integer>`) to one of the pool's threads and returns immediately with a `Future`.
`f.get()` **blocks** the main thread until the task finishes, then returns its value. (It throws checked exceptions, so the enclosing method must handle or declare them.)
`shutdown()` lets the pool's threads end so the program can exit.

steps.title: Race conditions
steps.body:
`count++` looks like one step but is three: **read**, add one, **write**. If two threads read the same value at the same moment, one update is lost.

Fixes, from simplest:

- **Don't share** — have each task return its result and combine them afterwards.
- **Atomics** — `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` is a single indivisible step.
- **Locks** — `synchronized` blocks or `ReentrantLock`.
- **Concurrent collections** — `ConcurrentHashMap` instead of a shared `HashMap`.

choices: Often less than 10000, and different from run to run
steps.hint: Is `count[0]++` one indivisible step?
steps.explanation: Eight threads perform unsynchronized read-modify-write on the same slot, so some increments overwrite each other. The result is usually **below 10000** and varies between runs — a classic race condition.

steps.prompt: Which change makes the count reliably reach 10000?
choices: Use an `AtomicInteger` and call `incrementAndGet()` in each task
Use more threads so it finishes faster
steps.explanation: `incrementAndGet()` performs the read-add-write as one atomic step. `final` only stops the variable being reassigned, more threads make collisions more likely, and sleeping just hides the bug sometimes.

steps.prompt: What does `pool.shutdown()` do?
choices: Stops accepting new tasks; already-submitted tasks still run to completion
Blocks until every task has finished
steps.explanation: `shutdown()` is a polite close: no new tasks, existing ones finish. It doesn't wait — use `awaitTermination` for that. `shutdownNow()` is the one that interrupts running tasks.

steps.prompt: This should print `142` and then let the program exit. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Exception in thread "main" java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException: Task java.util.concurrent.FutureTask@... rejected from java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor@...
  ...
steps.hint: What does a pool do with new tasks once `shutdown()` has been called?
steps.explanation: `shutdown()` means *accept no new tasks*, so the `submit` on line 4 is rejected with `RejectedExecutionException`. Call `shutdown()` once, after the **last** submit: task `b` is accepted, both results arrive and the pool's threads end. Deleting `shutdown()` prints `142` but the program never exits, because the pool's threads keep waiting for work. `shutdownNow()` rejects new tasks too, and `awaitTermination` only waits for the pool to finish: line 4 is still rejected afterwards.

steps.prompt: Which `Future` method blocks until the task's result is ready?
steps.explanation: **`get()`** waits for the result (there's also an overload with a timeout). Calling it right after submitting turns async work back into a blocking wait, so call it only when you actually need the value.

steps.prompt: The first task takes half a second; the second finishes almost instantly. What does this print?
steps.hint: The tasks finish in one order, but which thread prints, and in what order does it ask?
steps.explanation: Both tasks run at the same time on the pool's two threads, and `fast` finishes first. But only the main thread prints, and it calls `slow.get()` first, which **blocks** for about half a second until `slow` is ready. Then `fast.get()` returns at once, because that result is already waiting. Output order follows the order of your `get()` calls, not the order the tasks finish.

lessons.title: CompletableFuture pipelines
lessons.takeaway: CompletableFuture chains async steps: thenApply to transform, thenCompose to chain another async call, thenCombine to merge two.

steps.title: Async pipelines (Java 8)
steps.body:
A plain `Future` can only be waited on. A **`CompletableFuture`** lets you describe what happens *next*, without blocking:

- `supplyAsync(() -> ...)` — start a task (by default on the shared common pool)
- `thenApply(f)` — transform the result (like `map`)
- `thenCompose(f)` — chain another async call (like `flatMap`)
- `thenCombine(other, f)` — merge two independent results
- `thenAccept(c)` — consume the result
- `exceptionally(f)` / `handle(f)` — recover from errors
- `join()` — wait for the final value (throws unchecked exceptions)

steps.title: A small pipeline
steps.problem:
What does this print?

```java
CompletableFuture<String> greeting = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> "java")
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
    .thenApply(s -> "Hello, " + s);
System.out.println(greeting.join());
```
steps: `supplyAsync` produces `"java"` on a background thread.
The first `thenApply` turns it into `"JAVA"`.
The second turns that into `"Hello, JAVA"`.
`join()` waits for the whole chain and returns the final value.

steps.explanation: The two futures run independently; `thenCombine` waits for both and applies `Integer::sum` to their results: 20 + 5 = **25**.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `parseInt("oops")` fails, so the future completes exceptionally. `thenApply` is **skipped** for failed stages, and `exceptionally` replaces the failure with -1.

steps.prompt: `fetchUser(id)` returns `CompletableFuture<User>` and `fetchOrders(user)` returns `CompletableFuture<List<Order>>`. Which expression has type `CompletableFuture<List<Order>>`?
steps.hint: `thenApply` is like `map`; which one is like `flatMap`?
steps.explanation: `thenApply` would wrap the inner future, giving `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<List<Order>>>`. `thenCompose` flattens it. `thenAccept` gives `CompletableFuture<Void>`, and `join()` returns a plain `User`, which has no `thenApply`.

steps.title: CompletableFuture vs virtual threads
steps.body:
Long async chains were the main way to avoid blocking scarce platform threads. Since **Java 21**, virtual threads make blocking cheap, so straightforward code like `var user = fetchUser(id); var orders = fetchOrders(user);` inside a virtual thread is often clearer.

`CompletableFuture` is still handy for combining independent results and for APIs that already return futures — and you'll see it everywhere in Java 8–17 codebases.

lessons.title: Virtual threads in practice
lessons.takeaway: Use one virtual thread per blocking task (Java 21+), limit resources with semaphores rather than pools, and don't expect speed-ups for CPU-bound work.

steps.title: Why virtual threads?
steps.body:
A classic **platform thread** is an operating-system thread: heavyweight, so a server can only afford a few thousand. A thread blocked waiting for a database is wasted.

A **virtual thread** (final in Java 21) is managed by the JVM. When it blocks on I/O, it **unmounts** from its carrier OS thread, which then runs another virtual thread. So you can have **millions**, each written as simple blocking code.

They shine for **I/O-bound** work (HTTP calls, database queries). They don't make **CPU-bound** work faster — you still have only as many cores as you have.

steps.title: 10,000 sleeping tasks
steps: Each task gets its **own** virtual thread — 10,000 of them is no problem.
`Thread.sleep` blocks the virtual thread, which unmounts and frees its carrier for other tasks. All 10,000 sleep at the same time.
Leaving the try block calls `close()`, which waits for every task to finish.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body:
- **Don't pool virtual threads.** They're cheap — create one per task.
- **Limit access to scarce resources with a `Semaphore`** (or the resource's own pool, like a DB connection pool), not by capping threads.
- **Be careful with big `ThreadLocal` caches** — with millions of threads they multiply. Scoped values (final in Java 25) are the lighter alternative.
- **On Java 21–23, blocking inside `synchronized` pins** the virtual thread to its carrier; prefer `ReentrantLock` there. Java 24 removed this limitation.
- **Structured concurrency** (`StructuredTaskScope`) is still a preview in Java 25.

steps.prompt: You're moving each workload from a platform-thread pool to one virtual thread per task. Will it get a big throughput boost?
buckets: Little or no gain: cores are the limit

items.text: A web service where each request waits about 200 ms for a database
Calling three slow HTTP APIs for each of 5,000 orders
A chat server holding 50,000 mostly idle connections
Sending 10,000 emails, each waiting on a mail server
A tight loop that searches for prime numbers
Training a model on in-memory data

steps.hint: Does the task spend its time waiting for something outside, or computing?
steps.explanation: Virtual threads help when many tasks spend their time **waiting**: on a database, an HTTP API, a socket or a mail server. A blocked virtual thread unmounts, so thousands can wait at once without thousands of OS threads. Resizing images, searching for primes and training on in-memory data are **CPU-bound**: the 8 cores are the limit, not the number of threads. And a single-threaded program has nothing to run concurrently at all.

steps.prompt: Same 10,000 tasks that each sleep 1 second, but run on `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100)` (platform threads). Roughly how many **seconds** does it take?
steps.hint: How many tasks can be sleeping at the same moment?
steps.explanation: Only 100 tasks run at once, so 10,000 tasks need 10,000 ÷ 100 = **100** rounds of 1 second each. With virtual threads it's about 1 second.

steps.prompt: On Java 21, a teammate writes `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())` so at most 50 tasks hit the database at once. What's the recommended approach?
choices: One virtual thread per task, and limit database access with a `Semaphore` or the connection pool
Keep it — pooling virtual threads is the standard pattern
Add `Thread.sleep` calls to slow the tasks down
steps.explanation: Virtual threads are meant to be created per task, never pooled. Limit the **scarce resource** directly — a `Semaphore` with 50 permits or the connection pool — and let everything else run freely.

steps.prompt: On **Java 21**, a virtual thread does a slow network call while inside a `synchronized` block. What happens?
choices: It pins its carrier thread, which can't run other virtual threads until the call finishes
Nothing special — exactly the same as outside `synchronized`
steps.explanation: Before Java 24, a virtual thread blocking inside `synchronized` stayed stuck to its carrier (*pinned*), reducing throughput. `ReentrantLock` avoided it; Java 24 fixed it for `synchronized` too.

steps.prompt: Complete the factory method name: `Executors.________()` returns an executor that starts a new virtual thread for each task.
steps.explanation: **`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`** — typically used in try-with-resources so closing it waits for all tasks.
